newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary trade gap rise no danger for C/A-analyst.
newsitem.headline: Hungary trade gap rise no danger for C/A-analyst.

text.p: Hungary's foreign trade deficit could hit $3.5 billion in 1997 but should not adversely affect the current account figure, a research institute said.

"For 1997 we forecast an export growth of 10 to 12 percent and an import growth of 11 to 13 percent in dollar terms," Zoltan Torok, analyst at economic think-tank Kopint-Datorg Rt, told a news conference on Wednesday.

"This will mean an over $3 billion trade deficit by the end of the year but we don't think the rising trade deficit will endanger the current account deficit," he said, adding they expected the C/A deficit to be around $2 billion this year.
In 1996, Hungary's trade deficit amounted to $2.659 billion while the C/A deficit was $1.678 billion forints.
Kopint-Datorg forecasts Hungary's exports to rise to between $17.5 billion to $18 billion, while imports are seen reaching $21 billion.
The analyst said Hungarian exports will benefit from strengthening relations to the EU as well as from trade with countries in the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA).

"The 1997 economic outlook of developed countries and of the EU can be regarded as favourable, the economic growth of CEFTA countries continues, while the decline has stopped in the CIS countries -- all of which means a favourable outlook for Hungarian exports," Torok said.

"Nevertheless, as a result of rising domestic consumption and investments, and of amendments in the regulatory system, such as the abolishment of the import surcharge...we can expect a more substantial increase in imports," Torok said.
Hungary wants to phase out the import surcharge by July.
Hungary's finance ministry forecasts a trade deficit of around $2.5 billion and a current account deficit of $1.5 billion to $2 billion for 1997.
Hungary, an OECD member since mid-March 1996, generates roughly two-thirds of its trade with EU-countries.
Of Hungary's exports in 1996, the EU accounted for 68 percent, CEFTA seven percent and Russia, Belarus and the Ukraine for a combined seven percent, with smaller percentages going elsewhere.
In 1996, the EU was the source of 62 percent of Hungary's imports, CEFTA provided seven percent and Russia, Belarus and Ukraine combined had 12 percent, a table in Kopint-Datorg forecast showed.
